12875-life-in-the-roman-world-of-nero-an:
T. G. Tucker's 1924 survey, Life in the Roman World of Nero and St. Paul, rebuilds daily life in the first-century empire. Chapters cover the empire's extent, travel, provinces, emperor and senate, Nero, taxation, Rome's streets and water, town houses, country seats, furniture, social days, women, children, army, religion, philosophy, and art. Burial and tombs close the tour.

A peristyle description shows the method: marble tables, goldfish cisterns, fountains spouting from statuettes, and curtains for shade between columns. Tucker writes for general readers, not only scholars. The book remains a vivid guide to the world Paul and Nero shared.
15572-a-leap-in-the-dark-a-criticism-of-:
A. V. Dicey, fellow of All Souls College and former Vinerian professor of English law at Oxford, published this criticism of Home Rule in London in 1912, with John Murray. The first edition appeared in June 1893, on the Home Rule Bill of that year; this is the third edition. Dicey dedicates the book to Irish Unionists defending their rights as citizens of Great Britain and Ireland.

Chapter one contrasts the old constitution with the new one the bill would make. It traces Parliament's effective authority across the kingdom, the absence of federalism, and the bill's abolition of imperial authority in Ireland. Later chapters weigh federal features, limits on an Irish parliament, and means to enforce a federal compact. Dicey argues the bill is a leap in the dark: a new constitution, not a small reform, and a threat to the Union.
16307-the-ascent-of-the-soul:
Amory H. Bradford traces the growth of a soul through twelve short chapters, from its first waking to hindrances, stern discipline, fresh waking, and at last the goal. Christ, prayer for the dead, and the question of whether death ends all get their own chapters. The book was issued in New York in 1902.

Bradford writes as a preacher speaking to ordinary believers, not as a scholar piling up proofs. Poems and plain images carry much of the argument, and each chapter stands on its own. The tone is hopeful throughout: growth is slow, setbacks are normal, and the end is not loss but fuller life.
16744-pratt-s-practical-pointers-on-the-:
The Pratt Food Company of Canada issued this practical guide to the care of livestock and poultry, after nearly half a century in business. Its opening pages stress good will won by better products and whole-hearted, expert service to farmers. The firm's aim, it says, was to meet the needs of the trade and to share in the success of its customers.

The guide gives plain pointers for feeding, housing, and tending farm stock and fowl, in the voice of a feed firm that knows the barn. It reflects early 1900s farm practice, when company books taught as well as sold. Modern readers get a useful source on old farm care, and farmers of its day got a handy, plain manual.
17597-halil-the-pedlar-a-tale-of-old-sta:
Maurus Jokai, author of The Green Book and Black Diamonds, wrote this tale of old Stambul, translated from the Hungarian novel A feher rozsa by R. Nisbet Bain in an authorised edition. A third edition appeared in London in 1901 with Jarrold and Sons, and in New York with McClure, Phillips and Company. Its motto, sans peur et sans reproche, promises a fearless, blameless hero.

Halil the pedlar moves through old Constantinople, where trade, intrigue, and romance meet. Readers get a Hungarian master's Oriental tale, colourful and adventurous. The book suits readers of Jokai and of historical romance set in the Ottoman capital.
1762-the-consul:
Richard Harding Davis tells of old Mr. Marshall, who served the United States as consul in one posting or another for over forty years, appointed by Lincoln and then forgotten by every administration after. His distinction, once his pride, has become his epitaph, and younger men now eye his post.

The story follows Marshall as consuls, French colleagues, and a hurricane close in on his last days in office. Davis, himself a war correspondent, writes with sympathy for a servant of the state whom the state no longer notices. It is a small, sharp tale about loyalty, age, and the quiet end of a career.
1953-a-book-of-strife-in-the-form-of-the:
George MacDonald's Book of Strife, takes the form of the diary of an old soul. It gathers short meditations and prayers written across a year, each one a conversation with God about doubt, sorrow, and hope. MacDonald, the Scottish minister and novelist, writes as an old man looking back on a life of faith.

The entries are brief and personal, and their power lies in their honesty: a soul that argues with God, confesses failure, and returns to trust. The book has been a companion to many readers since its publication, and it remains one of MacDonald's most loved works, quietly devotional rather than doctrinal.
20797-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Bread and bakers start a plain piece in Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 445. Towns, it argues, might save cartage costs if local bakers served local folk alone. Such thrifty, everyday questions fill this July issue of the weekly.

Volume eighteen's run kept the journal's mix of essays, tales, and useful facts. The Chambers brothers built a vast readership on cheap, sound weekly parts. Each number is a time capsule of what plain British readers pondered. Number 445 shows its homely side, turning a loaf of bread into a chat on trade and cost.
20806-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Wild children found in India start a strange inquiry in Chambers's Journal, number 446. Cases from Europe set the frame for these newer reports from abroad. The writers pause first to scan the natural history of such finds.

Feral children drew keen interest in an age gripped by questions of human nature. This July number mixes that inquiry with the journal's usual tales and facts. The Chambers weekly aimed to inform as much as amuse. Number 446 shows its curious side at full stretch, weighing odd reports with a calm, probing tone that invites readers to judge.
21010-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Famed picture buyers have come, seen, and gone, sighs Chambers's Journal, number 444, on an art show. Praise flowed freely from their lips, it notes, though cash came in a thinner stream. Such droll, worldly notes fill this July number of the weekly.

Volume eighteen's run kept the Chambers mix of art, tales, facts, and verse. Cheap weekly parts carried that mix into homes that bought few books. Number 444 shows the journal's cultured side, at ease in galleries. Each issue still reads as a small, sane guide to what its week found worth a family's thought.
21126-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Issue No. 447 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, dated Saturday, July 24, 1852, sold for three halfpence and was conducted by William and Robert Chambers. The Chambers brothers built their journal to bring cheap, improving reading to working families. Its lead essay here calls women the Martyr Sex.

That essay argues that women have borne hardship and oppression through history with a fortitude men have never matched. Around it the weekly number packs the usual Chambers mix of information and entertainment for the people. A single surviving issue like this one preserves the look, price, and tone of mid-Victorian popular print.
21193-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Issue No. 448 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, dated Saturday, July 31, 1852, leads with an essay called Book-Worship. Its writer argues that a book belongs to the age and nation that produce it. Great books survive as landmarks of thought, yet they always wear the dress of their own time.

William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal as cheap, improving reading for the people. This number follows the book essay with the weekly mix of tales, facts, and verse its readers expected for three halfpence. Kept alone, the issue preserves how mid-Victorian Scots readers mixed serious essays with light reading in one paper.
21549-jacob-faithful:
Captain Frederick Marryat tells a Thames waterman's life in Jacob Faithful, published in 1834, his fifth book. Jacob is born and raised on a lighter, a small river barge, on the Thames in London. His father rules the deck, his mother is its queen, and Jacob is heir apparent.

Marryat left the navy in 1828 and wrote twenty-six books in twenty years. He claimed never to know, at each day's start, what he would write. Jacob's tale gives a close, lively picture of London and river life in the early nineteenth century. Many count it among the best of English sea-and-river fiction.
21674-the-making-of-a-soul:
Kathlyn Rhodes opens The Making of a Soul in a small Kensington flat on a wet night. Barry Raymond comes home at ten to a wood fire, a whisky tray, and the last post. A telegram in its tawny envelope lies in a conspicuous place, waiting for him.

Rhodes had written The Desert Dreamers and The Lure of the Desert for Hutchinson. Her tales mix romance with the pull of faith and the East. Barry's telegram starts a change that the title names plainly: the making of a soul. Drawing rooms, deserts, and hard choices carry a hero toward a new life.
21828-the-life-of-st-paul:
Paul stands as the thinker of Christianity and the missionary of the Gentiles in this short life by James Stalker, revised in 1912. Stalker opens by arguing that some men seem sent into the world for the exact hour they met. He sets Paul in that company, beside Luther and Knox in his opening pages. The book then follows Paul's place in history, his character, and his work.

Hints to teachers and questions for pupils frame the volume, which was made for classes and study circles. Stalker had also written a life of Jesus, and his touch is clear and warm. Maps and a foreword by Wilbert W. White support the text. It is a compact, teachable life of the apostle.
24155-lady-bountiful:
George A. Birmingham wrote this novel of west Ireland society, published by George H. Doran Company with copyright in 1922. Society there is tolerant of much, Birmingham notes: a man may drink heavily in public or sink toward bankruptcy and keep his caste. He may not marry his cook, and when old Sir Tony Corless does so, people stop going to Castle Affey and stop asking him to dinner.

Sir Tony's bride is Bridie Malone, daughter of the blacksmith at the gates, at least forty years his junior, who can sign her name but little more. His son Captain Corless, wounded early in the war and now an inspector under the Irish government, eyes the match with dismay. Readers get a comic study of rank, marriage, and small-county pride.
24406-the-price-of-a-soul:
William Jennings Bryan wrote this address, published by Funk and Wagnalls Company in New York and London in 1914. The publishers note that Bryan delivered it first at the Northwestern Law School Banquet in Chicago. Then he gave it as a commencement oration at the Peirce School in Philadelphia, and extended it into a lecture in 1909. Bryan opens with proof that the subject matters: Christ took it up, and he never took up trivial things.

When Christ took up a theme, it was worth considering, and Christ weighed the soul with a force no one can heighten. On one side he set the world and all it can contain, all wealth, fame, and happiness one can covet. On the other he put the soul, asking what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul. Readers get Bryan's question, pressed home.
25053-the-temptation-of-st-antony-or-a-r:
Gustave Flaubert's Temptation of St. Antony, in this Chicago edition from Simon P. Magee, follows the hermit through a night of visions in the Thebaïd. The opening sets the scene on mountain heights, where a crescent platform ringed with huge stones holds a mud and reed cell, flat roofed and doorless. Chapters lead from a holy saint through love and power, the disciple Hilarion, a fiery trial, all gods and all religions, the mystery of space, and the chimera and the sphinx.

Among the apparitions come the old Ebionites, dried like mummies, with dull glances and white eyebrows, speaking in quavering tones. They knew the carpenter's son, they say, were of his age, and lived in his street. They watched him model little birds from mud, help his father at the benches, and roll balls of dyed wool for his mother. Flaubert's pageant is learned, lurid, and strange.
27706-life-of-st-vincent-de-paul:
F. A. Forbes wrote this 1919 life of Saint Vincent de Paul for young and old, in the Standard-bearers of the Faith series. It follows the French priest from about 1581 to 1660, from peasant childhood in the Landes to the courts of Paris.

Chapters cover his captivity, work among galley slaves, missions, the Grey Sisters, and care for foundlings. Forbes presents Vincent as a man whose charity became organized service, and the book remains a readable introduction to one of France's best-loved saints. The opening chapter pictures the boy leading his father's sheep across the sandy Landes.
28591-poems-with-power-to-strengthen-the:
James Mudge compiled and edited Poems with Power to Strengthen the Soul for the Abingdon Press, in a revised and enlarged edition first printed in 1907. Ten printings followed through September 1934, and the dedication addresses lovers of good poetry and good character together. Mudge claims only a little place in that large company.

Subjects run from heroism, courage, independence, greatness, duty, and service through brotherhood, consecration, peace, and humility. Contentment, aspiration, prayer, affliction, love, hope, faith, and trust lead to God's care, will, and presence, then Jesus, life, age, and death. Indexes by author, title, and first line close a book meant for daily strengthening.
29451-the-romance-of-the-soul:
Lilian Staveley, author of The Golden Fountain, wrote this 1920 sequel on the soul and its search for God in the midst of daily life. Printed in London by John M. Watkins, it asks how plain men and women, busy with work and kin, can find peace without leaving the world or putting on showy piety. The soul, Staveley says, is frail as gossamer yet strong enough to stand in God's presence.

Short, lyrical chapters trace longing, prayer, and the slow growth of trust, urging readers to seek God in home duties and quiet hours alike. The book does not offer a system so much as a way of paying heed. Those drawn to prayer, stillness, and the inner life will find here a gentle, hopeful companion.
29460-the-electoral-votes-of-1876-who-sh:
David Dudley Field's 1877 pamphlet, printed by D. Appleton and Company of New York, asks who should count the electoral votes of 1876, what should be counted, and what remedy fits a wrong count. The votes had been cast, and the certificates lay in Washington or on their way. Field writes as a lawyer and citizen at a moment when the presidency itself hung on the count.

Field's plea is plain: a citizen's vote must be counted and given its due place, or the whole voting performance becomes ridiculous. The pamphlet speaks to the Hayes-Tilden crisis with urgency and legal care. Students of American elections will find a primary text on a dispute that still shapes how counts are judged.
30389-the-prayers-of-st-paul:
This volume from the Short Course Series gathers connected studies on the prayers of St. Paul, meant for preachers, congregations, lay readers, and Sabbath school teachers. The series preface argues that few will face long courses of expository lectures, while a short course of six or eight linked studies on one theme fits modern mental and ministerial life.

The book suggests subjects for future schemes of work and offers scholarly yet practical exposition of Bible history and doctrine. Office bearers and mission workers can use it as a study aid, and general readers can follow Paul's prayers as a guide to faith and prayer. It reads as a compact course, clear, focused, and built for group or private study.
30579-the-shepherd-of-my-soul:
Rev. Charles J. Callan of the Order of Preachers writes The Shepherd of My Soul, published in Baltimore in 1915 by John Murphy Company, printers to the Holy See. Contents follow the Psalm of the Good Shepherd through eleven chapters. They move from Christ the Good Shepherd and shepherd life in the Orient to the Lord as shepherd who gives all that is needed.

Later chapters trace green pastures, quiet waters, restored soul, paths of justice, the valley of the shadow of death, and rod and staff as comfort. A table before enemies, anointed head, overflowing cup, and goodness and mercy all the days of life close the psalm. Callan offers devotional exposition for readers who pray the psalm.
31326-the-wealth-of-echindul:
Noel Loomis's story, printed in Planet Stories in July 1952, follows Russell, a luckless swamp drifter, carrying the loot of the ages out of Venus. He comes up out of the Great Sea-Swamp covered in mud and slime, seaweed hanging from his cheap diving suit. Brine drips from arms that hang limp after forty days under its weight.

Small, just over four feet high and misshapen, he has crossed two hundred miles of deadly swamp on foot from the Red Lava Range's flaming craters. He pitches forward asleep in the sand before the ordeal ahead. The magazine's blurb asks who in the Pass, that legalized city of vice, would risk his neck to help him, setting up a tale of treasure and betrayal.
31340-the-colored-girl-beautiful:
E. Azalia Hackley's 1916 book, published by Burton in Kansas City, compiles talks given to girls in colored boarding schools. The opening talk happened at Tuskegee Institute because the Dean of the Girls' Department asked for it, with just an hour's notice and nothing prepared in advance. Hackley asked what to discuss, and the girls answered that they wanted to hear about love, real love, and beauty, real beauty.

For forty minutes she talked heart to heart, and as girls asked questions she jotted points so similar talks might reach other schools, until a request to print them produced this volume. Dedicated to colored women in whom she has faith and colored children whom she loves, the book is a warm, practical message on character and self-worth.
34134-the-great-mogul:
Louis Tracy's 1905 romance The Great Mogul sets its tale in Mughal India, around Nur Mahal and the court world of the Great Mogul. The story opens in grief and peril, with lovers and schemers caught in the power of a throne.

Scenes run from palace gardens and wedding nights to Burdwan, tests of loyalty, and flights from danger. Tracy writes for readers who want colour, daring, and romance, with Nur Mahal at its centre, and rank and pride setting the traps. Chase's pictures mark the high points, from a barred gate to a wedding-night return.
5079-ziska-the-problem-of-a-wicked-soul:
Marie Corelli's novel opens among the pyramids and sands of Egypt, where a party of modern travellers meets a mysterious woman who claims a link to an ancient Egyptian princess. Her presence unsettles the group, above all a painter drawn to her beauty. The story turns on reincarnation, old guilt, and a love that is said to reach across centuries.

Corelli sets Egyptian tombs, balls, and desert nights against questions of the soul: whether a wicked past can follow a person into a new life. The result is a lush, melodramatic romance of its era, part ghost story and part moral fable about desire, revenge, and fate.
9937-woman-s-institute-library-of-cooker:
Volume three of the Woman's Institute cookery course covers the heart of the meal: soup, meat, poultry and game, and fish and shellfish. It begins with soup itself, its value, its kinds, and the stock pot, before teaching the principal ingredients and methods.

Later sections explain how to choose and cook meats, birds, and fish, with attention to cuts, times, and serving. The Institute's plain teaching style gives reasons along with rules. Home cooks get a thorough, practical manual for the main dish, the part of dinner guests remember most.
a-book-of-strife-in-the-form-of-the-diar:
George MacDonald published his diary of an old soul in 1880, as the title page notes, with each printed page of verse facing a blank page for the reader's own thoughts. The dedication explains the design: his print is the seed, the reader's page the ground. The poems run day by day through the year.

Each short entry is a prayer or a wrestle, in seven-line stanzas, on faith, doubt, pain, and growing old in hope. January opens with a plea to do at last, with humbler heart, what youth promised. MacDonald's verse is plain and musical, and the diary has served many readers as a year-long devotional companion.
a-leap-in-the-dark-a-criticism-of-the-pr: Albert Venn Dicey criticizes the principles of home rule as illustrated by the bill of 1893. His first chapter treats old and new constitutions and Parliament's effective authority throughout the United Kingdom. Dicey, former Vinerian professor at Oxford, writes for Irish unionists defending their rights. The book calls home rule a leap in the dark.
britannica-1911-adam-paul:
Paul Adam (born 1862) was a French novelist. He was born in Paris on the seventh of December. His first novel, Chair molle, brought prosecution in 1885. The court acquitted him of the charge. He then worked with Jean Moreas on fiction. Together they founded the journal Symboliste. Adam came forward as symbolism's early defender. His novels are numerous and varied in kind.

Two works show his range clearly. Le mystere des foules studies the Boulangist movement. Lettres de Malaisie imagines future politics fantastically. In 1899 he began a long novel sequence. It traces the Napoleonic campaigns in fiction. The Restoration and Louis Philippe's government follow. Basile et Sophia, a Byzantine romance, appeared in 1900.
britannica-1911-barnaul:
Barnaul is a town of Asiatic Russia, in the government of Tomsk, standing on a plain edged by offshoots of the Altai Mountains, where the Barnaulka river meets the Ob. It lies 220 miles south of Tomsk, and its population in 1900 was 29,850. Founded in 1730 by A. Demidov, it is the capital of the Altai mining districts.

Smelting furnaces lead its works, with glassworks, a bell-foundry, and a mint besides. The 1911 Britannica entry notes a meteorological observatory set up in 1841, a mining school, and a museum rich in mineral and zoological specimens. A monument in the town honours Demidov, its founder.
britannica-1911-bert-paul:
Paul Bert (1833–1886) was a French physiologist and politician, born at Auxerre. He entered the École Polytechnique to become an engineer. He then studied law, and at last physiology. Under Gratiolet and Claude Bernard he found his field. He took medical and science degrees at Paris. Chairs at Bordeaux and the Sorbonne followed in 1866 and 1869.

After 1870 Bert entered politics on Gambetta's side. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him a firm foe of clericalism. He fought to free national education from religious sects. In 1881 he served as minister of education and worship. His science ranged over grafting, poisons, anaesthetics, and respiration. He also studied the sensitive plant and coloured light on plant life.
britannica-1911-bril-paul:
Paul Bril (1554–1626) was a Flemish painter born at Antwerp who made his career in Rome. His elder brother Matthew (1550–1584) had won success at the Vatican, and that draw pulled Paul to Italy to live and work beside him. When Matthew died, Paul took over his pensions and posts.

In skill Paul far passed his brother. He painted landscapes with a depth of light and shadow, the chiaroscuro effect, then little practised in Italy, and filled them with figures that were well drawn and finely coloured. One of his best works named is the Martyrdom of St Clement in the Sala Clementina of the Vatican. The notice is short, but it fixes his dates, his Roman base and the landscape gift that set him apart.
britannica-1911-broca-paul:
Paul Broca (1824–1880) was a French surgeon and anthropologist born at Sainte-Foy la Grande in Gironde on 28 June 1824. He loved higher mathematics early, but circumstances pushed him to medicine. Starting study in Paris in 1841, he rose fast: house-surgeon in 1844, assistant lecturer in anatomy in 1846 and professor of surgical anatomy three years later.

Fellow of the Faculty of Medicine in 1853 and professor of surgical pathology in 1867, he wrote valued treatises on cancer, aneurism and other subjects. In 1861 he announced his great finding: the seat of articulate speech lies in the left side of the frontal region of the brain. In the part still called the convolution of Broca. As founder of the Anthropological Society of Paris in 1859 and its secretary until death, he was practically the inventor of modern craniology, the study of skulls.
britannica-1911-bronsart-von-schellendor:
Paul Bronsart von Schellendorf (1832–1891) was a Prussian general born at Danzig in 1832. He entered the Prussian Guards in 1849, joined the general staff as a captain in 1861. After three years of staff service and a spell of regimental duty returned to the staff, lecturing at the war academy. He rose to major in 1865 and lieutenant-colonel in 1869.

In the war of 1870 he headed a section of the Great General Staff and conducted the first negotiations for the French surrender at Sedan. Colonel and chief of staff of the Guard corps after the war, major-general in 1876 and lieutenant-general with a division in 1881, he became war minister in 1883. His tenure to 1889 brought many reforms to the Prussian army, above all the introduction of the magazine rifle. In 1889 he took command of the I army corps at Konigsberg, and he died on 23 June 1891 at his estate near Braunsberg.
britannica-1911-cullen-paul:
Paul Cullen (1803–1878), cardinal and archbishop of Dublin, was born near Ballytore in county Kildare. Schooled at Carlow and at Rome, he was ordained in 1829 after a brilliant course. He rose to rector of the Irish National College in Rome. In 1848 he saved the Urban College's property under the American flag during the Mazzini revolution. In 1849 he was named to the primatial see of Armagh.

As papal delegate Cullen presided at the national council of Thurles in 1850 and took a strong line on education. Moved to Dublin in 1852, he broke with the hotter Nationalists and in 1853 barred his clergy from public politics. He opposed Fenianism steadily while calling himself an ardent patriot. In 1866 he became the first Irish cardinal. Churches, schools, a hospital, and a seminary in his diocese mark his energy as an administrator. He died in Dublin on 24 October 1878.
britannica-1911-fleming-paul:
Paul Fleming (1609-1640), German poet, was born at Hartenstein in the Saxon Erzgebirge on 5 October 1609, son of the village pastor. At fourteen he went to school at Leipzig and then studied medicine at the university. The troubles of the Thirty Years' War drove him away. He was lucky to join an embassy sent in 1634 by Duke Frederick of Holstein-Gottorp to Russia and Persia, with the traveller Adam Olearius as its secretary.

The mission returned to Reval in 1639, where Fleming became betrothed and chose to settle as a physician. He went to Leiden for a doctor's diploma but died suddenly at Hamburg on the way home, on 2 April 1640. Though of the school of Martin Opitz, his lyric poems carry a ring of true feeling and religious fervour rare among his contemporaries. He was happiest in the sonnet. His German poems appeared after his death, in 1642.
britannica-1911-howson-john-saul:
John Saul Howson (1816–1885) was an English divine, born at Giggleswick-in-Craven, Yorkshire, on the 5th of May 1816. Schooled at Giggleswick, where his father was headmaster, he went to Trinity College, Cambridge, and there tutored the marquis of Sligo and the marquis of Lorne. Ordained in 1845, he became senior classical master at Liverpool College under his friend Conybeare, and succeeded him as principal in 1849.

Howson held that post until 1865, and a like college for girls at Liverpool owed much to his influence. In 1866 he took the vicarage of Wisbech, and in 1867 became dean of Chester Cathedral. There he threw himself into restoring the crumbling fabric, collecting nearly £100,000 in five years. His sympathies lay with the evangelical party. The account closes with his writings, above all the life of St Paul he shared with Conybeare, long a standard work.
britannica-1911-lacroix-paul:
Paul Lacroix (1806–1884), French author and journalist, was born in Paris on the 27th of April 1806, the son of a novelist. He is best known as P. L. Jacob, bibliophile, or "Bibliophile Jacob," a name drawn from his constant interest in public libraries and books. He was a prolific and varied writer. More than twenty historical romances alone came from his pen, besides serious histories that include a life of Napoleon III and an account of the Tsar Nicholas I of Russia.

With Ferdinand Séré he produced Le Moyen Âge et La Renaissance (1847), five volumes on the manners, customs and dress of those ages, prized chiefly for its great number of illustrations. He wrote many monographs on the history of culture, much bibliography, and, under the name Pierre Dufour, the Histoire de la Prostitution of 1851–1852. He died in Paris on the 16th of October 1884.
britannica-1911-leroy-beaulieu-pierre-pa:
Pierre Paul Leroy-Beaulieu (born 1843) was a French economist. He was brother to the writer treated just before him. Saumur was his birthplace, on 9 December 1843. Paris schools and law study came first. Bonn and Berlin followed. Back in Paris he wrote for Le Temps and other reviews.

Prize essays marked his rise. One of 1867 weighed how workers' minds move wages. Three more prizes came in 1870, on colonies, on rule in France and England, and on land tax. A finance chair came in 1872. In 1880 he took the Collège de France chair of his father-in-law, Michel Chevalier. His books count the cost of modern wars in men and wealth. Others treat women's work, wealth shares, and the modern state. In 1873 he founded the Économiste français.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-gau:
An entry on the Church of Gaul, which first appears in history during the Lyons persecution under Marcus Aurelius in 177. Pagan crowds rose against the Christians, and forty-eight martyrs died under torture. Among them were the slave Blandina, the youth Ponticus, the noble Vettius Epagathus, and the physician Attalus of Pergamum. The Christians of Lyons and Vienne wrote to Smyrna, and Eusebius preserved their letter as a gem of Christian literature.

Missionaries most likely came by sea to Marseilles and up the Rhône to Lyons, the metropolis of Gaul. The firm planting of the faith came from Asia: Pothinus, bishop of Lyons, was a disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna, as was his successor Irenaeus. Lyons stayed the centre of the Gallic Church, and Irenaeus intervened when Pope Victor sought to impose the Roman Easter on the churches of Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-franc:
Etienne-Francois, Duc de Choiseul, was a French statesman, born 28 June 1719 and dead in Paris 8 May 1785. Until thirty-seven he pursued a military career as the Comte de Stainville, marrying the daughter of Crozat, the financier, in 1750. So caustic was his speech that he was called the original of Gresset's Méchant. He found no favour at court until he served Madame de Pompadour by exposing d'Argenson's scheming to make Madame de Choiseul-Romanet the mistress.

He transmitted to the favourite a letter from Madame de Choiseul-Romanet proving the conspiracy. Madame de Pompadour rewarded him with the embassy to Rome in 1754. He held this post from November 1754 to January 1757, during France's contest between parliament and clergy over the Bull Unigenitus. In 1752 Parliament condemned priests who exacted confession certificates from the sick, and deprived appelants, who refused the Bull, of the sacraments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faculties-of-:
Faculties of the Soul rests on four plain facts about the mind. Consciousness changes without cease, its processes come in varied order and last but briefly, and they differ by felt character and by organ. Yet shared traits let us group mental states into classes. More lies in mind than shows in consciousness, since latent images resurface after long gaps.

Minds differ in power, not just in content, and all processes belong to one conscious self. These facts ground faculties, from Latin facere, to do, also called capacities or powers, the Scholastic potentiae. Two extremes fight over them. One treats faculties as real secondary agents that explain facts, as if sight worked because we have vision. The other grants them no reality at all, calling them mere labels. Saint Thomas steers between them, holding that faculties act only by the soul's energy and are not agents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-crep:
Francois Crepieul, born at Arras on 16 March 1638 and dead at Quebec in 1702, was a Jesuit missionary to the Montagnais Indians of Canada and their vicar apostolic. Educated at Jesuit colleges in Arras and Douai, he joined the order at Tournai in 1659 and studied at Lille and Douai. He taught at both places and sailed for Canada in 1670. After theology at Quebec College he was sent in October 1671 to Tadousac, where for twenty-eight years he laboured among the Montagnais and Algonquin peoples with untiring devotion.

He told his brethren that a Montagnais missionary's life was a tedious, prolonged martyrdom, and that journeys and native cabins were schools of patience, penance, and resignation. For fellow missionaries he wrote practical instructions from long service, printed in volume sixty-three of Thwaites's Relations, including a valuable account of the Calumet Dance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-eugene:
Michel-Eugene Chevreul, chemist, physicist, and philosopher, was born at Angers on 31 August 1786 and died at Paris on 9 April 1889. Schooled at Angers's Ecole Centrale, once the university, Chevreul went to Paris at seventeen and found a place in Vauquelin's laboratory, a chemical manufacturer's, later becoming its chief. At twenty he began publishing science, and at twenty-six became professor at the Lycee Charlemagne.

Later he directed the Gobelins, joined the Academy of Sciences, and entered the Legion of Honour, climbing every rank until the Grand Cross. His centennial jubilee in 1886 was a remarkable state-directed demonstration, which Chevreul met with bodily and mental vigour. His funeral, two years and seven months later, honoured his memory greatly. Though famed for wide-ranging work, his name rests chiefly on two lines of inquiry: in chemistry, The Constitution of the Fats, and in physics, The Harmony of Colours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mossul:
Mossul, seat of a Chaldean archdiocese, a Syrian diocese and an apostolic mission, stands on the right bank of the Tigris opposite ancient Nineveh, growing as Nineveh decayed across the river. Its Arabic name El-Mosil means the junction, and it is not the Mosel of Ezekiel, a mistranslation of Uzzal in northern Arabia.

Near its gates in 627 Heraclius broke Persian power at Nineveh, and the town then passed to Arab caliphs, Hamdanids, Beni-Okail, Beni-Mervan and Seljuk Turks. Melek-Shah built schools and academies, Zengi's son Nur ed-Din raised fine buildings, Saladin took it after 1174, and the Mongol Hulagu seized it in the thirteenth century. The entry follows its bishops, churches and missions down to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-paul:
Saint Paul here means the Minnesota archdiocese, not the apostle: a vast see stretching across the southern half of the state from east to west. Petitioned at the Baltimore council of 1849 and erected on 19 July 1850, it first covered some 166,000 square miles, the whole Minnesota Territory. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia recounts how a frontier village see grew into a metropolitan archdiocese.

Early bishops built parishes, schools, and seminaries for settlers pouring into the new territory, and the see was later divided as daughter dioceses split away. The entry lists counties, bishops, churches, and institutions, giving a snapshot of Catholic life in Minnesota on the eve of the First World War. Readers tracing the Church on the American frontier will find the groundwork laid out in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saul:
Saul, Hebrew for one asked for, was Israel's first king, son of Kish of Benjamin. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sets aside debates over sources and retells the story from two traditional accounts, which differ above all on his election and his fall from favour. That frankness suits a life told twice over in Samuel.

Samuel, last of the great judges, grew old, and his sons, given civic and religious rule, proved unfaithful. The people, unhappy, asked Samuel for a king like other nations. Samuel resented the plea, and God called it an offence, a virtual rejection of His own rule, yet told the prophet to grant it. The entry follows Saul from anointing through wars and disobedience to his death, showing a king chosen, used, and cast aside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Saint Paul, now styled of Chartres, began at Chartres in 1704. Monsignor Maréchaut, a theologian of Chartres Cathedral, founded them with Mademoiselle de Tilly and Mademoiselle de Tronche. Their first house had once belonged to a maker of wooden shoes. Members took annual vows for three years, then perpetual simple vows.

Dispersed during the Revolution, the congregation was restored by Napoleon I, who gave them a monastery at Chartres once owned by the Jacobins, earning them the name Sisters of Saint Jacques. They settled in England in 1847 at Cardinal Wiseman's invitation, and by 1907 counted fifty-six houses there, each with a school. They also ran hospitals in French colonies, schools in the Philippines, and houses in Siam.

The Sisters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul, also called Daughters of Charity, Servants of the Sick Poor, began in France in 1633. Vincent de Paul founded the congregation with Louise de Marillac, widow of Antoine Le Gras, for corporal and spiritual works of mercy. Their members took simple vows, not solemn ones, and served the sick poor in their homes, hospitals, and asylums.

In 1640 the sisters took complete charge of a hospital at Angers, and in 1641 their headquarters moved to a house opposite Saint Lazare. Four sisters took the first simple vows on 25 March 1642, pledging poverty, chastity, and obedience for one year. During the Fronde wars they fed and sheltered thousands of poor in Paris, and on battlefields in Poland they earned the name Angels of the Battlefield. By 1660 they counted more than forty houses in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-sa:
Founded in May 1833, the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul is an international association of Catholic laymen serving the poor personally. Eight young Sorbonne students met in the office of the Tribune Catholique to plan a society for Parisian poor. Frederick Ozanam conceived the project, with Père Bailly, the paper's editor, as first president. The founders answered Saint-Simonian taunts that Christianity bore no fruit by forming a Conference of Charity.

Members visit the poor in their homes and assist them by every means, without distinction of creed or race, serving the poor, sick, infirm, and unemployed. Bailly's founding principle held that charity must give moral assistance, not merely alms. Meetings open and close with prayer, minutes are kept, and personal visiting remains a condition of active membership. The society's work spans fresh-air outings, day nurseries, prisoner visiting, employment bureaus, immigrant care, and orphan homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-soul:
The soul, in Greek psyche and Latin anima, stands at the centre of philosophy because belief in life after death hangs on it. And this long entry defends its reality against rival theories. It defines the soul as the inward principle by which we think, feel. And will, and by which our bodies live, with mind naming that principle as the seat of conscious states.

Substantiality means this principle can stand on its own, while spirituality means it is not composite, extended, or bodily in nature. The entry argues each point in turn, answers the theories that would dissolve the soul into the body or its functions. And ties every step to the doctrine of immortality that gives the question its urgency.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gerard-bis:
Gerard, bishop of Toul from 963 to 994, became true founder of his see's temporal power while shunning court comfort. Born at Cologne in 935 to a wealthy, noble family, he was schooled for clerics there and lived as a model of obedience and piety. Ordained priest, he edified Cologne, then succeeded Gauzelin at Toul by Cologne's archbishop, welcomed by clergy and people. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Toul to 23 April 994.

He avoided long visits to Otto II's court, though the emperor wished him near, yet won confirmation of Toul's privilege as an independent state under imperial protectorate alone. That privilege, granted to Gauzelin by Henry the Fowler, made Gerard founder in fact of the bishops' temporal rule. He bore his office's burdens without its comforts, and the entry honours a bishop who governed by staying home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul:
Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, dominates this vast Catholic Encyclopedia article, which treats his life, letters, and theology at length. Born Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee and persecutor, he met the risen Christ near Damascus and turned to preaching the Gospel he had opposed. After Arabia, Jerusalem, and Antioch, he carried the faith through Asia Minor, Greece, and Rome.

Sections weigh the chronology of his journeys, the apocryphal Acts, and his teaching on Christ, redemption, and the moral life. His epistles, his clash and concord with Peter, and his martyrdom under Nero close the survey. Readers find biography, criticism, and doctrine combined, with the article's scale matching its subject's weight in Christian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vincent-de:
Vincent de Paul, founder of the Lazarists and the Daughters of Charity, remade French charity in the seventeenth century. Born at Pouy in Gascony in 1580, though some authorities say 1576, to a peasant family, he studied humanities at Dax with the Cordeliers and theology at Toulouse, graduating there. Ordained in 1600, he tutored while continuing study.

Sailing from Marseilles in 1605, Turkish pirates captured him and sold him at Tunis, but he escaped in 1607 with his master, a renegade he converted. Returning to France, he served as almoner to Queen Marguerite, took the parish of Clichy, and entered the Gondi household. There he found his mission among galley slaves and country poor, founding the Congregation of the Mission in 1625 and the Daughters of Charity in 1633. He died at Paris on 27 September 1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-john-and-:
John and Paul were martyred at Rome on 26 June, in a year no one can fix. This entry starts from what is certain: they were Roman martyrs whose tomb, under a basilica on the Caelian Hill, drew veneration as early as the fifth century. The house above it once belonged to the senator Byzantius and his son Pammachius.

Their Acts are pure legend, making them eunuchs of Constantina, daughter of Constantine, secretly beheaded at Julian's command in their own house. How their bodies reached that house in the fourth century remains unknown. Yet the church that took their names, titulus Byzantii, kept their memory alive for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-faithful:
Fully initiated Christians, called the faithful from Latin fideles or faith, are the people defined in this entry. Those bound to a religious body, accepting its doctrine and initiated into its rites, earn the name. Among Christians it marks those fully initiated by baptism and, regularly, confirmation, pledged to profess faith in Christ, proclaim his teachings, and live by his law.

Papal documents love the term Christifideles, faithful of Jesus Christ. Christian and faithful now differ little, since adult baptism grows rare and catechumenate has merged with baptism liturgically. Latin Church practice, by contrast, splits confirmation and first communion from baptismal initiation, while the primitive Church kept initiation in two acts, often years apart.
doe-osti-2588617-validation-of-numerical:
Yan Cao, Donny Hartanto, Ahmed Abdelhameed, and colleagues at Argonne National Laboratory wrote this validation report, ANL-ART-312, for sodium fast reactor simulation tools. Their ground truth is old but gold: SEFOR, the Southwest Experimental Fast Oxide Reactor. It ran from 1969 to 1972. Its experiments measured Doppler reactivity feedback from about 350 degrees Fahrenheit up toward the melting point of mixed oxide fuel, near 5,000 degrees.

Modern codes were lined up against the archived data. Monte Carlo tools MCNP, Serpent, and Shift modeled four SEFOR core configurations. So did the legacy ARC suite, the NEAMS code Griffin, and the system code SAS4A/SASSYS-1. Comparisons covered criticality, reflector worth, and kinetics parameters. They also covered isothermal feedback at zero power and power-ascending feedback, as output rose from 0.4 to 17 megawatts. Agreement with experiment was generally very good. Fiscal 2026 work will chase the modeling issues found.
doe-osti-2997226-high-temperature-gas-co:
Argonne and Idaho national laboratories report ANL/NSE-25/64, also numbered INL/RPT-25-88104, demonstrates linked simulations for high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. Lead authors Zhiee Ooi, Thanh Hua, and Hansol Park cover pebble bed designs, where fuel flows slowly through the core as coated spheres. Modeling such a reactor joins neutron behavior, heat flow, and whole-plant response at once.

Work inside the Griffin code made streamline-based pebble modeling easier to set up. An equilibrium fuel injection test case was rerun, on-the-fly cross-section generation was tried, and control rod behavior was studied. System-level runs with the SAM code model heat moving between channels, driven by pressure gaps that arise from temperature differences. Pebble cross flow, which carries heat from the hot inner core outward, is a named modeling target. Designers gain checked tools before hardware exists.
doe-osti-2997411-abbr-final-report-self-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2012112, by Yuhao Li, dated October 2025, closes a two-year project on artificial water channels for desalination. Living cells move water through protein channels that pass water fast and hold salt back. The project built synthetic molecules that self-assemble into similar channels, aiming at membranes that copy that trick.

More than twenty candidate channels were made and tested, including ring-shaped supramolecular assemblies and nanographene pores with atom-precise structure. Small chemical changes gave direct control over pore size and inner chemistry, which in turn set water flow and salt rejection. University partners collaborated on parts of the work. As an abbreviated filing, the report states aims, the candidate count, and the governing finding, with fuller data in project records.
doe-osti-3004273-mississippi-s-strategic:
Hillary K. Fishler and Varisara Tansakul, with collaborators Joe Hagerman and Pierre Andrews, present a state strategy study in Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2025/4140. The subject is Mississippi's electric grid. Flooding and tornadoes strike the state often, and its grid is aging, with a legacy of underinvestment in rural areas and floodplains. Long outages after storms are the recurring cost.

Using the TASTI-GRID platform and working with the Mississippi Development Authority, the authors build a multi-systems resilience strategy. Emergency coordination across local, county, and regional levels is one weakness they target. The study ties energy security to economic development: reliable power is part of what the state sells to residents and businesses. It is an overview document, meant to align state partners before detailed engineering begins.
doe-osti-3006495-development-of-calcined:
Oak Ridge CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2025/4195, dated September 2025, develops calcined clay and calcium sulfate blends for limestone calcined clay cement, or LC3. Denise Antunes da Silva and Paula Bran Anleu wrote it. The U.S. cement industry faces supply chain strain and high energy use, and calcined clays are supplementary materials. Their catch is variability: clay chemistry and physics shift from source to source, which can upset hydration balance, flow, and admixture demand.

The team procured five calcined clays, two Portland cements, limestone, gypsum, and a polycarboxylate dispersant. Isothermal calorimetry and mini-cone flow tests set the sulfate and dispersant demand for each mix. About 6.7 percent gypsum, relative to calcined clay weight, balanced sulfate consumption across every system studied. Dispersant demand, by contrast, varied significantly with clay source, so the report argues admixture strategies must be tailored clay by clay. Appendices graph the sulfate balance and dispersant dose results.
doe-osti-3030209-interplay-of-gas-phase-: Secondary organics got gas-phase-interplayed, and this DOE text studies multiphase growth. The pages detail the state findings. The chemists get their data. The dynamics were growth. The data were chemist. The organic were secondary. The state were phase.
doe-osti-3398698-impacts-of-electric-spa: Juneau heating got electric-impacted, and this DOE slides cover multifamily apartments. The pages detail the space findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The Juneau were apartments. The multifamily were space.
doe-osti-3440651-understanding-and-predi: ELMs got edge-predicted, and this DOE text covers high confinement turbulence. The pages detail the understanding findings. The physicists get their data. The regimes were reactor relevant. The data were physicist. The ELM-free were confinement. The turbulence were edge.
doe-osti-3683718-kauhale-o-k-papa-kahiki: Kahikinui's resilience center gets a second name here: Kauhale ʻO Kīpapa. Like the Halau Uma report, this summary covers technical assistance for the Maui community's cultural, learning, and resilience center design. The work supports a building rooted in Hawaiian community life.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in:
A cable dated July 8, 1999, sums up the Manila Air case in this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The cable went from New York to security staff and to posts in Bangkok, Islamabad, Manila, and Riyadh. Manila Air was the probe into a plot found in Manila, in the Philippines, in January 1995.

The plot, the cable says, was to plant bombs on airliners. One of its men was a top-ten fugitive by 1999. The sampled pages trace links abroad: a man reported to be living in Sharjah with his family, and word from Gulf security staff who said they would share what they learned. One man had been questioned about a Muslim group and then deported. The cable shows the bureau working the case through partner services years before the September 11 attacks.

A fax from the bureau's Los Angeles support office to San Diego, dated July 2002, carries this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The cover sheet is strict: the facts inside are for lead work only, are not to be passed to foreign governments, and may be stored only without credit to their source.

The pages that follow give a primer on Al Qaeda and its leader. They tell how the Afghan war shaped Usama Bin Laden's views and gave him a sense of purpose. The primer credits Al Qaeda with about twelve training camps in Afghanistan. As many as 5,000 men, it says, passed through them. Cells, it adds, had been planted in fifty countries, and some trained men may live as sleeper agents among local people.

A full Federal Bureau of Investigation report dated July 18, 2003, tests a press claim: that Al Qaeda made millions from conflict diamonds in West Africa. The claim came from a Washington Post series that began in November 2001. The Post said Al Qaeda men, based in Monrovia, Liberia, sold diamonds mined by the Revolutionary United Front from 1999 to 2001.

The bureau's finance team worked the claim in the United States and in Ghana, Belgium, Sierra Leone, and Burkina Faso. One theme, the report says, ran through the talks: people mixed up Al Qaeda and Hizbollah, and used the two names as if they were one. That mix-up sits at the heart of the report's caution. The report is a check on a news claim, worked on the ground in four countries.

One short cable, dated July 31, 2004, is the whole of this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. San Diego sent it to the Director's office as its response to the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks. The case name is the Mihdar file, the San Diego case on Mohdar Mohamed Abdullah. The cable's one lead is brief: read and clear. The rest is routing, case numbers, and marks of secrecy. A long San Diego case thus closed out with a one-line task, in the summer the commission's own report came due.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th:
A national threat warning message, sent over the law enforcement teletype system in July 2001, opens this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The Counterterrorism Division sent it to all regions. It states plainly that it is not a formal threat advisory, and that it should stay inside law enforcement hands.

The message reports a rise in threat talk in recent weeks from groups tied to, or in sympathy with, Usama Bin Laden. It says the bureau had no word of a firm threat inside the United States, but that an attack could not be ruled out. The near Independence Day holiday, it warns, might add risk. Later pages tell of a briefing for a federal protection group in Washington, where members weighed tighter security at federal sites.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CollacchiPaul_C:
On September 10, 1993, an assassination researcher wrote to Paul Collacchi of Menlo Park, California. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text, but the letter's contents sketch him plainly enough: he discusses his new book and his long history of filing Freedom of Information lawsuits.

FOIA litigation was the research movement's crowbar, and its veterans compared suits the way fishermen compare catches. A letter to a California reader in 1993 belongs to the last years of the mail era, just before the Assassination Records Review Board began releasing files in bulk. The letter is preserved as part of the movement's correspondence, its author lost but his trade unmistakable.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KangasPaul_Kang:
A tabloid-style publication titled Coup d'Etat Behind the Guns of Dallas claims the Kennedy assassination was solved. Its charge is dramatic: two high-ranking CIA assassins were photographed as tramps in Dealey Plaza. Neither the publisher nor the author is identified in the record.

The three tramps of Dealey Plaza photographs fed decades of identification games. A publication claiming to name two of them as CIA killers sold certainty where evidence was thinnest. The piece preserves that claim in its original tabloid form, useful as a record of what the market for answers would print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SpicaJohnPaul_S: Roy Wilkins, head of the NAACP, publicly denied a damaging claim about his role in the King case. A news article reports his denial that he served as an FBI contact in a campaign to discredit Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The charge struck at Wilkins's standing as a civil rights leader. His denial, kept in the files, shows how fiercely that reputation was defended.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TaylorPaul_Tayl: Assistant District Attorney Andrew J. Sciambra sent a memo to his boss, Jim Garrison, on May 28, 1968. It reports his interview with Paul Taylor, part of the New Orleans investigation into the Kennedy assassination. Garrison's office produced many such interview memos while building its case against Clay Shaw. The memo preserves one conversation in that effort, written for the district attorney's own files.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_CIA:
Senior CIA officials once offered ten thousand dollars to a pilot willing to arrange an accident on a flight carrying Raúl Castro. The plane was to fly from Prague to Havana. This briefing book, posted in April 2021, publishes the formally top secret documents behind that offer.

The pilot was already a recruited CIA asset inside Cuba. He asked for a promise that his own family would be cared for if he died in the crash. The posting calls it the earliest known CIA assassination plot against leaders of the Cuban revolution, and the paper shows how casually it was priced.
halil-the-pedlar-a-tale-of-old-stambul:
Mór Jókai, Hungary's great romancer, wrote Halil the Pedlar as A Fehér Rózsa, The White Rose, and R. Nisbet Bain translated it in this authorized edition. The scene is old Stambul under Sultan Achmed, in the tulip age of the Ottoman court. Halil is a humble pedlar; Gül-Bejáze, the White Rose, is the slave girl at the tale's heart. Chapters move from the pedlar's rounds to the camp and the bursting forth of the storm.

Tulip bulbs and human heads, as one grim chapter head has it, were both cheap in that Stambul. The tale builds toward the rising in which the historical Patrona Halil shook the throne. Jókai mixes harem intrigue, street life, and revolt in his richest manner.
jacob-faithful:
Captain Frederick Marryat published Jacob Faithful in 1834, a novel told by Jacob himself. Jacob was born on a lighter on the Thames at low water, he begins. His father was monarch of the deck, his mother queen, and he heir-apparent. Orphanhood follows a trifling accident in the first chapter heads.

A captain's wife shelters the boy after a mishap in a later confession scene. She had sent for his mother against his father's wish, it emerges. Mary bursts into tears as the tale comes out. River life, service, and fidelity carry Jacob from the lighter into the wider world.
life-in-the-roman-world-of-nero-and-st-p:
T. G. Tucker surveys Roman daily life in this 1924 volume. His period runs from Nero's reign through St. Paul's world. Opening chapters map the empire's extent, travel, and provinces. The imperial system of emperor, senate, knights, and people follows.

Later chapters enter Roman houses, furniture, and country seats. Readers follow an aristocrat's social day from morning to dinner. Middle and lower class life, holidays, and amusements get equal space. Women, children, education, and the army complete the social picture. Roman furniture and the country homestead receive separate chapters. The army, military service, and public careers close Tucker's survey.
nasa-tm-19650025647-a-simple-equation-fo:
R J Simoneau and R C Hendricks at Lewis Research Center offered a simple equation for a common heat problem in this 1964 paper. When a gas flows fast through a heated tube, it picks up heat by turbulence. Engineers need a reliable rule to predict that transfer. Their equation pulls together, or correlates, test results in one compact form.

The paper was prepared for a heat transfer meeting in Cleveland in August 1964. A good correlation saves each designer from repeating the same tests. Heated tubes appear in engines, reactors, and test rigs of many kinds. A simple, checked rule for their behavior had wide practical value at the time.
nasa-tm-19700022468-current-nasa-researc:
Eugene J. Manganiello of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 aeronautical congress in Rome, Italy. It surveys the turbojet propulsion research then under way at NASA. The Lewis center had been growing this work for five years, he notes.

The effort covers each main engine part in depth. Inlets, compressors, combustors, turbines, and nozzles all had active programs. The goals were lower weight, lower fuel use, and steadier running. Such gains matter for all aircraft, Manganiello states. They matter most for high-performance planes that fly at high Mach numbers.
nasa-tm-19700025056-coordinate-system-in:
NASA issued this Manned Spacecraft Center internal note on how the choice of coordinate system affects a trajectory problem. The problem is the regularized trajectory optimization problem, a math form used to find the best flight paths. Coordinate choices sound like bookkeeping, but they can change how hard the computing becomes.

The note sets out the formulation, then discusses results across a long central section before drawing conclusions. Its tables use one test case throughout: the optimal low thrust Earth escape spiral. For that spiral, the tables compare numerical integration behavior at three levels of error bound separation. Five appendices carry supporting detail that the main text draws on.
pratt-s-practical-pointers-on-the-care-o:
The Pratt Food Company of Canada issued this handbook of practical pointers on the care of livestock and poultry as a service to the farmers who bought its feeds and remedies. A preface boasts of nearly half a century of business service and the good will of customers, won by better products plus expert, personal, whole-hearted service. The introduction then argues the economics: animal husbandry is the sure foundation of profitable, permanent agriculture.

Where herds are kept and their manure goes back to the fields, soil grows richer, crops increase, and the farmer prospers with his land. Livestock also spreads labor and income across the whole year, whether the money crops are meat, milk, or eggs. Between the advertising frame sits husbandry advice, the kind companies gave away to bind customers. The book documents an era when a feed firm could pose as the farmer's professor.
the-ascent-of-the-soul: Title pages and a contents start present The Ascent of the Soul by Amory H. Bradford, printed at New York by the Outlook Company in 1902. Bradford is billed as author of Spirit and Life, Heredity and Christian Problems, The Growing Revelation, and other works. He gives the book to the memory of his father. A verse from In Memoriam stands at the front, on the soul's seeming separate wholeness. The contents open with The Soul on page 1 and The Awakening of the Soul on page 25.
the-consul:
Richard Harding Davis opens his story on old man Marshall, who has served the United States as a consul somewhere in the world for over forty years. President Lincoln named him to the service. For twenty-five years that fact was his mark of honor; by the story's present it has become the shield that keeps his post.

Each new government brings place-hunters hunting spoils on the map, yet the State Department will not touch a man Lincoln named. Marshall never complains of exile, bad climate, or being pushed down to worse posts to make room for men with pull. When a politician demands his share of the trough, the Secretary of State offers him Marshall's current post. Three of the last six consuls quit within a month and three died of yellow fever.
therese-story-of-a-soul:
Thérèse of Lisieux, a French Carmelite nun, wrote her life story in notebooks at her sisters' request. She died in 1897, aged twenty-four, and the book appeared the next year. Thomas Taylor's English version spread it across the Catholic world.

Thérèse sets out her 'little way': trust in God through small acts of love, not great deeds. Her childhood memories and convent days are told with disarming honesty. The book made her one of the most widely read saints of modern times. She was canonized in 1925 and named a Doctor of the Church.
woman-s-institute-library-of-cookery-vol: Volume Three of the Woman's Institute Library of Cookery covers soup, meat, poultry and game, and fish. Pages present here hold a contents list, but no recipes or lessons. The soup section lists stock making, clear soups, cream soups, purees, and chowders. The meat section promises beef cuts, steaks, roasts, stews, and gravy making. Later sections on poultry and fish appear in the volume title, beyond the list shown here.
ziska-the-problem-of-a-wicked-soul:
Marie Corelli published this novel in New York in 1897. She dedicated it to the living reincarnation of a figure called Araxes. The prologue opens under a full moon at the Great Pyramid. The Sphinx seems to drowse in grey sand. At midnight a voice cries Araxes across the desert silence. A shadow slips from the tomb's portals and takes a woman's form.

Her eyes flash with unholy fire as she vows pursuit through life and death. Reincarnation and revenge drive the tale from its first page. Egypt's ruins give the story its stage. Readers get a gothic romance about a wicked soul hunted across ages.
